1.3.7.20 The Irrelevance of Collective Adoption to Binding Status
Objection: 'These Regulations cannot bind because the People have not collectively adopted them.'
Response: This objection confuses two distinct concepts: (a) the existence of the regulatory framework, and (b) the number of persons operating under it.
The Second Amendment requires the existence of 'a well regulated Militia.' It does not require a minimum membership threshold. A fire department exists when it has equipment, protocols, and at least one trained firefighter—not when it has 1,000 members. A lifeboat exists when it is built, equipped, and has at least one occupant capable of operating it—not when it is full. The building does not cease to be a fire station because only one firefighter has arrived. The lifeboat does not cease to exist because only one passenger has boarded. The Constitution does not ask how many showed up. It asks whether the thing exists.
A fetus is a human life from conception, though it takes nine months to develop into an infant capable of independent existence. It does not become human at birth—it was human before, and birth merely changes its capacity, not its nature. Similarly, the Militia exists from the moment it has regulations and at least one member. Growth changes capacity, not existence.
These Regulations are the equipment and protocols. You are the first occupant. Therefore, a well regulated Militia exists. The requirement is satisfied.
Additional occupants increase capability. They do not increase existence. Existence is binary. Once TRUE, it cannot become 'more TRUE.' A thing either exists or it does not. There is no third state of 'exists but needs more people to count.'
The Ninth Amendment prohibits any construction that would deny the right to a well regulated Militia during any period when the framework exists but collective adoption is incomplete. To say 'these Regulations are not binding until ratified by others' is to say 'your right to a well regulated Militia is denied until enough other people show up.' That is precisely the construction the Ninth Amendment forbids. It makes your right dependent on the actions of others—exactly what the Bill of Rights was designed to prevent.
The critic says: 'The solution is that the People can, through any collective process including informal consensus, adopt regulatory frameworks.' But what collective process exists when no framework has been adopted? What informal consensus can occur when the People have no shared text to discuss? The critic's solution assumes the very thing that is absent—an organized People capable of collective choice. The infinite loop is real. The critic offers no escape from it.
Therefore: These Regulations bind from the moment of promulgation and individual adoption. Collective adoption increases capability. It does not create legitimacy. Legitimacy existed the moment the constitutional command was obeyed. The Second Amendment does not say the Militia is necessary once ratified by enough people. It says the Militia is necessary. Necessary means necessary now. Binding means binding now. These Regulations are fully legitimate, fully binding, and fully operative from the moment of promulgation and individual adoption. Nothing added by others can make them more legitimate than the Constitution already makes them.

1.3.8.1 Doctrine Definition
The Revolutionary Necessity Doctrine holds that when a positive constitutional requirement, particularly one declared necessary to the security of the free state, goes unfulfilled for multiple centuries due to collective inaction, it creates a constitutional void that threatens the very order the Constitution was instituted to secure. In such a condition of prolonged and systemic default, the reserved power to fulfill that requirement may, and of necessity must, be exercised by individual members of the sovereign People to prevent the Constitution from becoming a nullity in that particular. This doctrine is not an assumption of power but the mandatory exercise of a reserved power during a state of constitutional emergency caused by neglect.

The application of this doctrine to these Regulations is dispositive:

(b) The Duration of Default: Two hundred and fifty years, from ratification in 1791 to the present. This represents the entire post-ratification history of the United States.
(c) The Location of the Remedial Power: The power to "regulate" the Militia in the comprehensive sense is not delegated to the United States (as established in Section 1.3.4) and is therefore reserved to the People by the Tenth Amendment.
(d) The Nature of the Collective Failure: The failure is absolute, prolonged, and uncontested. No entity—federal, state, or collective popular—has produced the required regulations based on the 1787-1791 text.
(e) The Constitutional Result: In this precise circumstance, the individual exercise of the People's reserved regulatory power becomes not merely permissible, but constitutionally mandatory to cure the default and secure the free state.

1.3.11: The Individual's Portion of Reserved Sovereignty
When property is held by "the people" as common owners, each person holds an undivided interest in the whole. Any co-owner may use the common property for its intended purpose, provided they do not exclude others from their equal right to use it. The reserved power to regulate the Militia is such property—held by the People as co-tenants in common. The exercise of that power by one co-tenant does not negate the ownership of all; it uses the common asset to fulfill a duty that benefits all. The other co-tenants retain full authority to participate, amend, or supersede the use through collective action (Section 11). This model answers the collective-action objection directly: individual action is not usurpation but lawful use of commonly held power by one of its owners when the others have defaulted in their duty to maintain the property. Each Person holds a portion of the People's sovereignty, and when the collective body is dormant regarding a constitutional duty, individual portions may activate to fulfill what the Constitution requires.
Note on the Historical Foundations of This Model
The co-tenancy framework used in this section may appear to import property law concepts into constitutional analysis. In fact, it recovers the legal reasoning the founding generation itself applied.
Sir William Blackstone's Commentaries on the Laws of England — the single most consulted legal text among the founding generation, cited in constitutional debates more frequently than any other source — treated fundamental rights through property frameworks as a matter of course. The right to exclude government from one's home was understood through the common law concept of the castle. The right to keep arms was intertwined with the property right to possess instruments of defense. Blackstone did not treat these as separate domains of law. Neither did the Framers.
More directly, founding-era political theory routinely described sovereignty itself in property terms. The people hold the radical title to all governmental authority. They delegate certain defined estates to government — the enumerated powers. They retain the reversion: all powers not conveyed return to the grantor. These were not mere metaphors. They were technical legal concepts, drawn from conveyancing and trust law, applied to explain how constitutional authority is structured and how it flows.
John Locke, whose Second Treatise shaped the Declaration of Independence and the constitutional framework it preceded, described the people's power to reconstitute government as a trust relationship with legal incidents derived from property law. When the trustee violates the terms of the trust, the power reverts to the beneficiaries — a term of art from property law, applied to political theory by the source the Framers themselves cited.
The Framers applied this framework directly. In Federalist No. 46, Madison described the people as the common superior of both state and federal government — the ultimate sovereign whose retained authority checks both. He wrote that the people hold 'the transcendent and precious right' to alter or abolish government, a right that pre-exists and supersedes any governmental structure. This is the property model: the grantor retains authority over what was never conveyed. The enumerated powers are the conveyance. The Tenth Amendment's reservation is the reversion clause. The People are always the grantor in possession of what was never transferred.
In this context, treating the People's reserved power as a form of tenancy in common is not an innovation. It is an application of the legal vocabulary the Founders used, grounded in the sources they cited. What the Tenth Amendment reserves to the People, they hold in common. What is held in common may be used by any co-tenant for its intended purpose, subject to the equal right of all others and subject to the collective authority of the whole to govern its use going forward. The Ninth Amendment ensures that no construction requiring impossible collective preconditions may defeat this right. Together, the two amendments confirm what property law already supplied: a reserved power held in common is available to any co-tenant when the purpose it serves demands exercise and the collective body has not acted.
1.3.11.1 — The Co-Tenancy Model in Founding-Era Legal Thought
The co-tenancy model is not a modern analogy imported into constitutional law. It is the legal framework the founding generation itself used to understand the relationship between the People and their governments.
Sir William Blackstone's Commentaries on the Laws of England — the single most cited legal authority in the ratification debates — describes joint tenancy as a form of ownership in which each tenant holds "the whole and every part," such that the possession of one is the possession of all. 2 Blackstone, Commentaries *179–193. When the Constitution reserves a power to "the people," it creates the sovereign equivalent: an undivided interest held by each member in the whole. Any member may exercise the commonly held power for its intended constitutional purpose. That exercise does not exclude the other holders; it fulfills what belongs to all for the benefit of all.
James Wilson — signer of both the Declaration and the Constitution, delegate to the Philadelphia Convention, and one of the original justices of the Supreme Court — made this framework explicit. In his Lectures on Law (1790–1792), Wilson described the People as holding the radical title to all governmental authority. Governments hold only delegated powers as tenants. The reserved powers remain with the People as the reversionary interest — the title that returns when the tenant exceeds the grant.
The co-tenancy model applied here therefore recovers the founding generation's own vocabulary. The People hold the radical title to Militia regulation. Congress was never the tenant for that power. The Tenth Amendment is not creating a new reservation; it is confirming one that was never conveyed. The reversionary interest never left.

1.3.15 The Sole Constitutional Mechanism for Fulfilling the Necessity
The Second Amendment declares a well regulated Militia to be necessary to the security of a free State. This necessity is absolute, present-tense, and non-deferrable.Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 grants Congress the power to organize, arm, and discipline the Militia. However, the Constitution deliberately omits the word “regulate” from Clause 16 while using it in Clause 14 for the land and naval forces. By the plain text, the comprehensive power to regulate the Militia was not delegated to Congress.Under the Tenth Amendment, all powers not delegated to the United States are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people. Because the power to regulate the Militia was not delegated, it is reserved to the people. 
No mechanism exists in the Constitution for any private citizen, group, state, or Congress to create binding national militia regulations other than the reserved power of the people themselves. There is no Article V process, no congressional statute, no state compact, and no judicial ruling that can lawfully create the singular national “well regulated Militia” required by the Second Amendment.
Therefore, the first faithful exercise of the People’s reserved power to regulate the Militia constitutes the only known constitutional mechanism to fulfill the necessity declared in the Second Amendment.These Regulations are that first faithful exercise. They are the only possible way the constitutional requirement can be met under the text as written.

1.3.16.11 The Ratification Analogy Refuted
Objection: 'The original Constitution required ratification by the people in convention. Therefore, these Regulations require similar collective ratification before they can bind.'
Response: A law that has been on the books for 233 years requires something. No one has complied for 233 years. The first person finally complies. Is that person 'creating new law'? No. They are obeying old law. Their obedience is valid the moment it occurs, not the moment others recognize it. A fact does not become true because it is acknowledged. It was true before. A couple's wedding vows require collective participation—two people consenting before witnesses. But once married, the duty to remain faithful does not require daily re-consent by both parties. If one spouse remains faithful while the other strays, the faithful spouse is not 'creating new marriage' by continuing to honor the vows. They are obeying the existing vow. The Constitution's commands are vows. They were made in 1788. They do not need to be remade. They need only to be kept.
These Regulations are obedience to a 233-year-old command. They are binding because the command was always binding and is now, finally, being obeyed.
The objection conflates two constitutionally distinct acts:
The Founding Act (1787-1788):
      * No supreme law existed prior to the Constitution's ratification
      * The People were creating something from nothing
      * Collective action was required because the act was constitutive—bringing into being the very framework of government
The Fulfillment Act (These Regulations):
      * The Constitution has been supreme law since 1789
      * The Second Amendment has commanded a well regulated Militia since 1791
      * The power to regulate the Militia has been reserved to the People since 1791
      * Nothing new is being created—only what the Constitution already requires is being provided
Founding requires ratification. Fulfillment requires obedience. Different acts, different requirements.
Constitutional commands do not require re-ratification. When the Constitution commands 'Congress shall make no law' abridging speech, that command binds immediately upon ratification. No second ratification is required for each citizen to exercise free speech. When the Constitution commands that a well regulated Militia 'is necessary,' that command binds immediately upon ratification. The requirement exists. Only the content was missing. Providing that content is not a new founding—it is obedience to an existing command.
The Ninth Amendment prohibits applying the ratification analogy here. The people acted through elected delegates in state conventions—representatives, not the entire populace voting directly on each clause. The Constitution itself thus recognizes that the people may act through representatives and through individuals exercising delegated authority. 1.3.17 — The Ordinary Meaning of “Necessary” 
Five Proofs Made Explicit
Five independent constitutional grounds establish that the militia clause is operative, not merely prefatory. Each proof stands alone. Together they are conclusive. Any reader who encounters the claim that the clause is 'merely prefatory' or that this is a 'contested interpretive question' should consult these proofs directly before accepting that characterization.
(1) The rule against surplusage. Every clause in the Constitution must have independent legal effect. If the militia clause is merely prefatory — a historical note explaining the rationale for the right that follows — it has no independent legal effect. It becomes constitutional furniture: present, visible, and legally meaningless. The Constitution does not contain furniture. Every word was placed deliberately by drafters who debated structure at the clause level. A clause with no legal effect violates the foundational interpretive principle that every provision must mean something.
(2) United States v. Sprague (1931). The Supreme Court affirmed that the Constitution's words are to be understood in their normal and ordinary meaning as voters would understand them. Johnson's Dictionary (1755) — the authoritative reference available to the ratifiers — defines 'necessary' as 'such as must be; not free; indispensably requisite.' Under Sprague's command to apply ordinary meaning, 'necessary' is a command, not a comment. It declares an indispensable ongoing condition, not a preferred outcome.
(3) Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 — the structural proof. Congress was granted the power 'To provide for calling forth the Militia to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions.' This enumerated power presupposes the Militia's existence as a constitutional given. You do not enumerate a power to summon something optional. You do not build a calling-forth mechanism into the governing architecture of federal power unless you have guaranteed that the thing to be called forth will exist. The guarantee comes from exactly one place: the Second Amendment's declaration that a well regulated Militia is necessary. Clause 15 and the militia clause are the same constitutional requirement operating at two levels — the Second Amendment establishing that the Militia must exist, Clause 15 establishing how the federal government activates it once it does. To read the militia clause as prefatory decoration is to make Clause 15 a power with no mechanism attached — a lever connected to nothing. The Framers did not engineer contingent powers into the constitutional structure without guaranteeing what those powers depend on.
(4) The grammar of 'being,' addressed fully in this section. 'Being necessary' is a present participial construction that places the necessity beyond argument as a continuous given. The clause does not say 'having been necessary' or 'which may be necessary.' It declares an ongoing constitutional condition, operative at every moment from ratification forward.
(5) Heller's own limits. District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense. In doing so, Heller described the militia clause as 'prefatory' in the sense that it does not limit the operative clause's individual right. Heller explicitly did not decide questions about the militia clause's full independent scope or its ongoing constitutional obligations. Reading Heller's structural description as a ruling that the militia clause is legally void — with no independent operative force whatsoever — goes further than Heller went and produces a result Heller did not authorize. The individual right is secured. The militia clause's independent operative command remains unaddressed by Heller and is addressed here.
The Grammar of Necessity: What "Being" Does
The Second Amendment does not say a well regulated Militia is necessary. It does not say a well regulated Militia was necessary. It says a well regulated Militia, being necessary — and that single word, being, changes everything.
"Being" is an absolute participial construction. This is a specific grammatical form with a specific legal effect. When a writer uses this construction, they are not introducing a fact that requires proof or demonstration. They are stating a condition assumed to be already true and continuously operative — a background fact the rest of the sentence proceeds upon. The Framers did not choose "which is necessary" or "that is necessary," constructions that would have invited argument about whether the necessity existed. They chose "being necessary" — a construction that places the necessity beyond argument as a given, and builds the operative right upon it.
This has five consequences that no subsequent law can undo.
First, the necessity is temporally continuous. Present participles describe uninterrupted ongoing states. "Being necessary" means the Militia's necessity is true at every moment from ratification forward — not at some moments, not when convenient, not when recognized, but always and without pause. The obligation to fulfill it renews with every sunrise. There is no moment since December 15, 1791 at which the Second Amendment has not been commanding the existence of a well regulated Militia.
Second, the necessity is self-declared, not government-granted. "Being necessary" was not made true by Congress. It was not recognized into existence by the courts. It was not proclaimed by the executive. The supreme law declared it true and proceeded on that basis. This means the obligation to fulfill it does not depend on government action, government recognition, or government consent. It exists because the Constitution says it exists. It operates because the Constitution is the supreme law.
Third, the necessity is ontologically fused with the free state. The construction "being necessary to the security of a free State" means the secured free state cannot constitutionally exist without the Militia. This is not a policy preference. It is the constitutional structure of existence: if the free state is secured, the Militia exists; if the Militia does not exist, the free state is not secured. The word "being" is the hinge that makes this an existence claim, not an aspiration.
Fourth, the necessity is self-executing. Because it was not created by legislation, it cannot be suspended by legislation. Because it was not granted by courts, it cannot be withdrawn by courts. The present participle requires no enabling act. The Ninth Amendment reinforces this: no construction may deny or disparage rights retained by the People, including the right to have a thing the Constitution itself declares necessary to their security.
Fifth, and most important for binding effect: these Regulations do not create the necessity. They satisfy it. The necessity has been operating continuously since 1791. It was commanding compliance on every one of the 85,550 days before these Regulations existed. These Regulations are the act of obedience to a command that has never stopped being issued. The binding force is not the Regulations' own authority — it is the authority of "being necessary," which has been pending, unsatisfied, and continuously violated since ratification. The Regulations are not new law. They are the end of a 234-year violation of existing law. That is what makes them operative upon promulgation and not one moment later.
Any argument that these Regulations require additional process before becoming operative is an argument that a constitutional constant can be held in suspense. A constant does not wait. "Being necessary" does not pause for committees. It does not hold its breath for recognition. It commands. These Regulations obey. The command and the obedience together constitute the complete constitutional fact.
The Present Participle as Constitutional Emergency
The grammatical point established above has a further implication—one that transforms the 234-year default from historical fact into present emergency. The Second Amendment does not say a well regulated Militia was necessary. It does not say it will be necessary. It says a well regulated Militia, being necessary—present participle, continuous tense, operative at every moment from ratification forward without pause, without expiration, without exception.
A present-tense command cannot be deferred. To argue that "necessary" may wait for a more convenient political moment is to argue that a human being may defer the necessity of oxygen until conditions improve. The violation of the Second Amendment's command is therefore not something that happened once in 1791 and has since been tolerated. It is something happening right now. It happened yesterday. It will happen tomorrow if nothing is done. Each day without a well regulated Militia is not a historical fact—it is a present constitutional emergency renewing itself with each sunrise.
The 85,550 days of default are not 85,550 past events. They are 85,550 counts of a continuous present violation. The cure for a present-tense violation is not a future-tense promise. It is a present-tense act. That act is these Regulations. Now.
1.3.17.1 Ratification-Era Definition
The Second Amendment declares in present-tense language ratified in 1791: “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State…”At ratification, “necessary” carried the ordinary meaning established in Samuel Johnson’s Dictionary (1755): NECESSARY. adj.
Such as must be; not free; indispensably requisite.This understanding was shared by the founding generation. George Mason stated at the Virginia Ratifying Convention (June 14, 1788): “The militia is the necessary defense of a free state.”
1.3.17.2 The Constitutional Logic of Necessity
When the Constitution declares X necessary for Y, it establishes:
      * Y cannot exist without X
      * X must exist whenever Y exists
      * Absence of X = absence of Y
Applied: No well regulated Militia = no constitutionally secured free state.
1.3.17.3 The Command Is Immediate, Not Deferrable
The Amendment did not say “shall be necessary” (future) or “would be necessary” (conditional).
It said “being necessary” — present, declarative, operative.
The command took effect December 15, 1791 and has never been suspended.1.3.17.4 Existence Satisfies Necessity
The Constitution commands the existence of a well regulated Militia.
It prescribes no specific process.
Therefore:
      * When such regulations exist → command is obeyed
      * When they do not exist → command is violated
These Regulations exist. The command is obeyed. The necessity is satisfied.
1.3.17.5 Constitutional Injury Quantified
From ratification to promulgation: 85,550 days of continuous violation.
Duration does not convert violation into compliance. 
1.3.17.6 Sufficiency, Not Perfection
The Constitution requires the Militia to be well regulated — properly functioning and governed by established rules.
It does not require perfection.
These Regulations provide a complete constitutional framework. That is sufficient. That is compliance.
1.3.17.7 Necessary Does Not Mean 'Eventually’
The word 'necessary' in Johnson's Dictionary means 'such as must be; not free; indispensably requisite.' It does not mean 'eventually necessary.' It does not mean 'necessary after sufficient deliberation.' It does not mean 'necessary once enough people agree.'
If oxygen is necessary for human life, it is necessary NOW—not after committee approval, not after majority vote, not after government recognition.
If a well regulated Militia is necessary to the security of a free State, it is necessary NOW—not after collective ratification, not after congressional action, not after judicial blessing.
A patient bleeding out does not need a committee to study blood loss. They need a tourniquet NOW. A drowning man does not need a vote on whether water is wet. He needs a hand NOW. The free state has been drowning for 234 years. These Regulations are the hand. Do not ask the drowning man to wait for a quorum.
Any construction that delays the fulfillment of 'necessary' is a construction that denies the meaning of 'necessary.' The Ninth Amendment prohibits such constructions. The Constitution commands immediate existence. These Regulations provide immediate existence. The command is satisfied. The free state is secured. NOW.
The critic says: 'The proper path is slow, gradual adoption.' But necessary is not slow. Necessary is not gradual. Necessary is immediate. The critic's path may be reasonable for many things—but not for what the Constitution itself declares necessary. For that, delay is not an option. Delay is violation. Delay is suffocation. Delay is the very thing the Ninth Amendment prohibits.
1.3.17.8 — State Constitution Evidence That "Being Necessary" Was Operative Language
Critics relying on Heller's 'prefatory clause' framing argue that 'being necessary' is merely explanatory — a historical justification for the right that follows, not an independent command. This reading fails not only against the rule against surplusage, but against the plain evidence of how identical language was used in founding-era state constitutions.
The Pennsylvania Constitution of 1776, Frame of Government, Section 47, uses the near-identical construction: 'The right of conscience being necessary to the security of a free state, shall be held inviolable.' The grammatical structure is precise: 'being necessary' introduces a positive right — the right of conscience — that the constitution then protects with operative force. The clause is not decorative. It is not prefatory. The declaration of necessity is the constitutional finding that grounds and requires the protection that follows. The clause as a whole is operative.
The Pennsylvania Constitution of 1776 was not a historical artifact during ratification — it was the governing law of the Commonwealth, cited in debates, enforced by courts, and understood by every delegate who read it. This provision remained active, binding constitutional law at the precise moment the Second Amendment was being drafted and ratified. The founding generation was not reading it as a historical note. They were living under it as supreme law. When they used the same grammatical construction in the Second Amendment, they used language they already understood — through direct constitutional experience — to carry operative legal force.
This is the same construction the Second Amendment uses. 'A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State' is the constitutional finding. 'The right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed' is the operative protection that flows from it. The Pennsylvania precedent demonstrates that the Framers used 'being necessary' to establish an indispensable constitutional condition — not to offer an introductory comment that could be severed from legal effect.
The rule against surplusage therefore stands with historical confirmation: if the militia clause has no independent legal effect, the Framers used a recognizable operative construction — one they were simultaneously enforcing in state law — for purely decorative purposes. They did not. The clause means what it says and what the Pennsylvania Constitution proves it was understood to say: a well regulated Militia is a constitutional necessity. That necessity is a constitutional fact, not a suggestion, and it commands fulfillment.
1.3.18 Hierarchy of Constitutional Authority: Explicit Text and Necessary Application
TIER 1 — EXPLICIT TEXT 100% Binding:
All provisions directly citing and executing explicit constitutional language from the 1787-1791 Constitution. Tier 1 provisions derive their authority directly from the constitutional text itself, not from inference or interpretation. 
They include but are not limited to:
      * Gold and silver coin as sole legal tender (Article I, Section 10)
      * Militia exclusive enforcement of the Laws of the Union (Article I, Section 8, Clause 15)
      * Detention authority in cases arising in the Militia during public danger (Fifth Amendment)
      * Reserved regulatory power over the Militia (Tenth Amendment, via Clause 14/16 contrast)
      * Necessity of a well regulated Militia to the security of a free State (Second Amendment)
      * The People's right to keep and bear arms (Second Amendment)
      * Protection against unreasonable searches and seizures (Fourth Amendment)
      * Prohibition on denial or disparagement of retained rights (Ninth Amendment)
      * Supremacy of laws made in Pursuance of the Constitution (Article VI, Clause 2)
Tier 1 provisions are immutable absent a valid Article V amendment that does not deny or disparage rights retained by the People under the Ninth Amendment. No governmental entity—federal or state—possesses authority to nullify, supersede, or diminish Tier 1 provisions.
TIER 2 — NECESSARY APPLICATION Inference to Execute Tier 1:
All procedural specifications, structural details, and implementing mechanisms required to make Tier 1 authorities operational, effective, and safe. Tier 2 provisions derive their constitutional authority through necessary inference from Tier 1 text.
Tier 2 provisions include but are not limited to:
      * Detention review timelines and tribunal compositions
      * Asset seizure protocols and documentation requirements
      * Nullification review and approval procedures
      * Specific organizational structures not commanded by constitutional text
      * Funding request mechanisms and reporting requirements
Tier 2 provisions are binding as the lawful exercise of the People's reserved power to implement and execute their Tier 1 constitutional authorities. They are subject to collective refinement, amendment, ratification, or replacement by the organized Militia through the processes established in Section 11.
1.3.18.1 Constitutional Authority for Tier 2 Provisions
The authority to create Tier 2 provisions derives from the following constitutional principles:
(a) Necessary Incident Doctrine: When the Constitution grants an authority (Tier 1), it implicitly authorizes the adoption of reasonable procedures to make that authority operational, effective, and safe. An authority that cannot be exercised is no authority at all.
(b) Parity of Sovereignty: Article I, Section 8, Clause 18 authorizes Congress—a derivative sovereign holding delegated powers—to enact laws necessary and proper to execute its delegated powers. The People—the original sovereign holding reserved powers—possess at least the same latitude to adopt necessary implementing procedures for their reserved powers. The greater includes the lesser.
(c) Constitutional Completeness: The Second Amendment's declaration that a well regulated Militia is "necessary" requires not merely the existence of regulatory content (Tier 1) but also the procedural infrastructure to make such regulation operational (Tier 2). Proof of this requirement is set forth in Section 1.3.19.
All Tier 2 provisions derive their constitutional authority from these principles. They are not assumptions of undelegated power but necessary implementations of delegated and reserved powers.
1.3.19 The Completeness Theorem: Mathematical Proof of Constitutional Necessity
THE COMPLETENESS THEOREM
Let:
      * X = "a well regulated Militia" (the entity the Second Amendment declares necessary)
      * T = 234 years of constitutional default
      * E = the People (the entity in whom regulatory power is reserved)
      * P = the power to regulate the Militia (the Tenth Amendment reserved power)
Axiom 1 (Constitutional Command): The Constitution requires X to exist. (Second Amendment: "necessary")
Axiom 2 (Historical Fact): X did not exist for time T. (No comprehensive, nationally unified regulations existed prior to these Regulations.)
Axiom 3 (Power Location): The power to create X is not delegated to Congress (Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 omits "regulate") and is therefore reserved to E. (Tenth Amendment)
Axiom 4 (Power Exercise): E must exercise P to create X. (Logical necessity: if power exists and requirement exists, exercise is required to fulfill requirement.)
THEOREM: To exercise P without specified constitutional process, E must:
(1) DEFINE STANDARDS: Establish what "well regulated" means, what the "free State" is, and what threatens its security. Without definition, regulation has no content.
(2) ESTABLISH PROCEDURES: Create the rules, protocols, and mechanisms by which the Militia operates, governs itself, and executes its duties. Without procedures, regulation has no operation.
(3) CREATE SAFEGUARDS: Implement accountability mechanisms, review processes, and limitations on power to prevent abuse. Without safeguards, regulation becomes tyranny.
(4) ENABLE ENFORCEMENT: Provide remedies for violations, consequences for usurpation, and means to secure the free State against infringement. Without enforcement, regulation is advisory.
PROOF:
Step 1: If any of elements (1)-(4) is missing, P is not fully exercised. (Definition: regulation requires standards, procedures, safeguards, and enforcement.)
Step 2: If P is not fully exercised, X cannot exist. (Because X requires P by Axiom 4.)
Step 3: If X cannot exist, the Second Amendment's necessity requirement remains unfulfilled. (By Axiom 1.)
Step 4: Unfulfilled constitutional requirements constitute ongoing constitutional violation. (By definition.)
Step 5: Therefore, each element (1)-(4) is NECESSARY—its omission would perpetuate constitutional violation.
Step 6: Each element as implemented in these Regulations is PROPER—it incorporates and respects constitutional safeguards.
Step 7: Each element as implemented is MINIMAL—it imposes no greater burden than required to make P operational and safe.
CONCLUSION:
The Regulations of the Free State Militia contain no extraneous provisions. Every section, subsection, and clause is either: (a) explicit constitutional text applied directly (Tier 1); or (b) a necessary and proper inference required to make explicit constitutional text operational (Tier 2). The framework is complete. The requirement is fulfilled. The Constitution is obeyed.
COROLLARY 1 — Burden of Omission:
Any person or entity claiming that these Regulations contain unnecessary provisions must identify which of elements (1)-(4) is not required for X to exist, and must demonstrate how X could exist without such element. Failure to do so concedes the necessity of the challenged provision.
COROLLARY 2 — Mathematical Certainty:
This proof is deductive, not empirical. If the axioms are true (constitutional text) and the logic is valid (each step follows from previous), the conclusion is mathematically certain.
COROLLARY 3 — Sufficiency, Not Perfection:
This theorem proves sufficiency, not perfection. These Regulations are sufficient to fulfill the constitutional requirement. Refinement, clarification, and improvement are not only permitted but encouraged through the collective processes of Section 11. But the existence of potential improvements does not negate the sufficiency of the existing framework. The Constitution requires a well regulated Militia. These Regulations provide it. The requirement is satisfied.
1.4 Regulation by the People, Governance by Congress
Under the Second Amendment and by the reserved power confirmed in the Tenth Amendment (see §1.3), the People alone exercise the comprehensive power of Regulation—a power deliberately omitted from Congress's delegated authorities in Article I, §8, Cl. 16—over the greater body of the Militia that constitutes “A” well regulated Militia, exercising their certain right of sovereign authority to establish and maintain a single, unified set of regulations for its internal operations that is based wholly in the text of the Constitution without relying on unadopted positions of the forefathers. This regulation, rooted in the amendment's declaration of "A well regulated Militia," is an enumerated certain right of the People, not delegated to any other entity, no one else has the power of regulation the entire Militia specifically reserved to them, including the States or Congress. Congressional governance under Clause 16 applies only to Militia portions actively employed or about to be employed in federal service. This governance terminates upon completion of federal service duties.
Under the Tenth Amendment all Powers not reserved to the States or the Federal government are reserved to the People.  It includes:
      * Membership Criteria: Defining eligibility, qualifications, and requirements for joining the militia.
      * Rules and Discipline: Setting codes of conduct, disciplinary measures, and operational procedures.
      * Structure and Leadership: Determining the militia's organization, including ranks, leadership selection, and decision-making processes.
Pursuant to Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 of the Constitution, Congress shall exercise its authority to "provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the Militia" to prepare the Militia for potential federal service under Clause 15. This Congressional authority under Clause 16 to "provide for" organizing, arming, and disciplining concerns future provision of militia resources and governance. It is constitutionally distinct from Congress's Article I, Section 8, Clause 1 power "to pay the Debts" for services already rendered. The latter authority, governing compensation for constitutional labor performed to cure the 234-year "well regulated" default, is addressed in Section 11.1 and operates under separate textual authority. 


This authority shall be limited to:
      * Organize: Establishing structural frameworks for regiments, battalions, and companies.
      * Arm: Providing standard firearms, ammunition, and equipment to every militiaman at zero cost.
      * Discipline: Funding and implementing training programs for federal readiness.
      * Governing such Part of them as may be employed in the Service of the United States. Part not Whole.
      * Militia must be trained and readied by the Federal Government protocols given to their States under the Authority of training the Militia according to the discipline prescribed by Congress So as to be called into uniform Federal Service when necessary.
      * Militia governance by Congress shall terminate upon completion of that part's federal service obligations under Clause 16. 
      * This Congressional authority does not extend to regulation of the Militia's internal operations nor does it diminish the People's regulatory authority harmonized with State implementation per Section 1.3.2, definitions, membership criteria, Free State defense protocols against domestic enemies within government or non officer leadership selection, which are exclusively reserved to the People under the Second Amendment and Tenth Amendment. 
Failure to provide these resources constitutes Unconstitutional Disarmament under the Second Amendment.
When the Militia is called forth under Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 to:
      * Execute the Laws of the Union,
      * Suppress Insurrections, or
      * Repel Invasions,
Congress governs such part of the Militia as is and may be employed in the Service of the United States, with authority strictly limited to:
      * Serving the President.
      * Tactical deployment for law execution;
      * Resource allocation during suppression or repel missions;
      * Combat discipline in active engagement zones.
      * To be considered under this governance Congress must be paying the Militia Members under this governance directly and continuously for services and training pertaining to this governance.
      * This governance terminates upon completion of federal service. Congress governs the part of the  Militia actively 'employed as well as those about to be employed in the Service of the United States' (Art. I, §8, Cl. 16). This authority terminates when federal service ends.  
      * Congress's Clause 16 powers support, but do not supplant, the People's regulation, ensuring harmony for the free state's security.
Congress shall not:
      * Regulate membership criteria (Section 1.4);
      * Alter disciplinary codes for non-federalized units;
      * Appoint officers (reserved to States per Clause 16);
      * Delegate Clause 15 enforcement to non-Militia entities.
States' Exclusive Authority: The Tenth Amendment reserves to the States powers not delegated to the United States. Per Article I, Section 8, Clause 16, The People of the United States, exercising their sovereign authority under the Second Amendment's mandate for 'a well regulated Militia,' shall establish a single unified system for the Militia's regulations, membership, and discipline. The States, pursuant to Article I, §8, Clause 16, shall implement this system by:
      * Appointing officers from candidates certified under the People's national standards;
      * Conducting training strictly adhering to the Congress’s prescribed curriculum;
      * Enforcing no supplementary rules that fragment or contradict the unified framework.
States exercise substantive authority over appointments and training per Art. I, §8, Cl. 16, consistent with the People's unified regulations. They may enact supplementary regulations—such as local training protocols or logistical arrangements—provided these do not conflict with the People’s right to "A" unified set of regulations. Any State action that fragments the Militia or contradicts its national framework violates this right and is subject to Militia correction.
Congress’s power to ‘provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining’ (Art. I, §8, Cl. 16) is strictly ministerial and logistical. It does not extend to defining the Militia’s character, membership, or sovereignty, which are vested solely in the People by the Second Amendment and retained under the Ninth and Tenth Amendments.


This structure ensures the Militia remains "well regulated" as a singular, citizen-led force under the People’s authority, with Congress providing support and States contributing within defined limits, all consistent with the constitutional mandate to secure the free state. This right is absolute and cannot be diminished by Congress or the States
The National Guard’s Unconstitutionality
The National Guard violates the U.S. Constitution’s mandates to secure the free state. The Constitution, under Article I, Section 8, Clauses 15 and 16, and the Second Amendment, establishes the Militia as a citizen controlled, citizen-led force working alongside the States and Federal government to execute Union laws, suppress insurrections, repel invasions, and secure a free state—where the Constitution governs, rights are inviolate, and government is limited. 


The National Guard, created by federal law (Militia Act of 1903), deviates from this design in several ways:
         * Dual ControlIts dual state-federal command structure, allowing federalization beyond the Constitution’s enumerated purposes (Clause 15), undermines the people’s rights and state authority, exceeding congressional power and violating the Tenth Amendment.
         * Federal Funding: Its fiat federal funding and permanent integration into the military structure surpass Congress’s limited power to organize and arm the militia (Clause 16).
         * Undefined "Free State": The National Guard lacks a constitutional definition of "free state", they don’t even know what a Militia defends. How can they secure the free state when they don’t have regulations that even mention it? They are not well regulated as is required by the Second Amendment.  
         * Usurpation: By assuming the Militia’s exclusive role (Clause 15) without being "well regulated" by the people, it usurps the constitutional militia’s mandate and undermines the rights reserved to the people. 
The National Guard is thus unconstitutional, lacking the state-centric, citizen-led structure intended by the framers and failing to secure a free state. The Free State Militia rejects it as a legitimate entity and asserts its sole authority as the constitutional Militia.


1.4.1 Awaiting Congressional Discipline Standards
Pursuant to Article I, Section 8, Clause 16, Congress retains the delegated power "to provide for...disciplining the Militia." This power concerns the establishment of uniform training methods, tactical doctrines, and operational procedures for Militia forces when called into federal service.
Congress has not exercised this power for 234 years. The Militia hereby requests that a Constitution-compliant Congress provide such discipline standards at the earliest opportunity.
Until such standards are provided, the Militia shall:
        (a) Train according to constitutional principles and sound military doctrine;
        (b) Coordinate with State training authorities pursuant to their Clause 16 reservation;
        (c) Maintain readiness for federal service under Article I, Section 8, Clause 15.
This absence of congressional discipline standards does not diminish the Militia's existence, as "discipline" (training methods and tactical doctrine) is constitutionally distinct from "regulation" (governance framework, membership criteria, and free state defense protocols), which is reserved to the People per Section 1.3.
Historical Clarification: The Militia Act of 1792 and What It Actually Did
The Militia Act of May 8, 1792 is sometimes cited as evidence that comprehensive militia regulations already existed, or that Congress once exercised the power to 'regulate' the Militia. A careful textual analysis using Johnson's Dictionary (1755) — the same source that defines 'necessary' for the Second Amendment — demonstrates the opposite: the 1792 Act exercised only the three ministerial powers Clause 16 delegates to Congress, while leaving the comprehensive regulatory power untouched in the People's hands.
Johnson's Dictionary defines the four relevant terms as follows:
Organize: 'to form with suitable organs; to construct.' The 1792 Act organized the Militia into divisions, brigades, regiments, battalions, and companies — structural frameworks. This is Clause 16 authority.
Arm: 'to furnish with weapons of offence.' The 1792 Act required each militiaman to provide his own musket, bayonet, cartridge box, and equipment. This is Clause 16 authority.
Discipline: 'to educate; to instruct; to keep in order.' The 1792 Act prescribed muster days and training exercises based on Baron von Steuben's Regulations for the Order and Discipline of the Troops of the United States. This is Clause 16 authority.
Regulate: 'to adjust by rule or method.' The 1792 Act did not define the Militia's fundamental character or purpose. It did not define 'free State.' It did not establish the governing framework the Second Amendment requires — the standards by which the Militia identifies threats to constitutional order, the protocols by which it operates, the principles by which it secures the free State. It performed the ministerial functions Clause 16 assigns to Congress. It did not touch the comprehensive regulatory function reserved to the People.
That the First Congress — including Framers — exercised only Clause 16's three enumerated powers and no more confirms, rather than undermines, the Clause 14/16 distinction. They knew what Clause 16 gave them. They used exactly those powers. The comprehensive regulatory function was left where the Constitution placed it: with the People.
Furthermore, the Act was never operative. It imposed duties on every free, able-bodied male citizen between eighteen and forty-five but provided no enforcement mechanism. Within a decade it was universally ignored. A law that is universally unenforced is not a regulation — it is a proposal. Constitutional existence requires operative effect. The Act produced none.
The Act was explicitly repealed by the Dick Act of 1903, which divided the Militia into the organized National Guard — a select corps bearing no meaningful resemblance to the constitutional Militia — and the unorganized remainder with no regulations at all.
The 1792 Act is therefore confirmation of the 234-year default, not a cure for it. It shows that Congress knew its role and stayed within it. It shows that comprehensive regulation never occurred. It shows that the People's reserved power remained unexercised for the full 234 years from ratification to these Regulations.
The 1792 Act: Congress's Duty, Not the People's
The Militia Act of 1792 is often cited as evidence that the People's regulatory duty was already fulfilled. It was not. The Act performed Congress's three delegated functions under Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 — nothing more and nothing less:
What the 1792 Act DID:
— Organized the Militia into divisions, brigades, regiments, battalions, and companies
— Purported to 'arm' the Militia by requiring each man to provide his own musket, bayonet, cartridge box, and equipment — at his own expense, through his own procurement, with no supply from Congress.
— Disciplined the Militia by prescribing muster days and training exercises based on Baron von Steuben's manual
What the 1792 Act did NOT do:
— Define the 'free State' or what the Militia exists to defend
— Fulfill Congress's own constitutional duty to arm the Militia.
— Establish governing standards for identifying threats to constitutional order
— Create the foundational regulatory framework the Second Amendment requires
The 1792 Act is therefore the template for Congress's Clause 16 duties — not a substitute for the People's reserved regulatory power. It organized, armed, and disciplined exactly as Clause 16 authorizes. Its failure to regulate confirms the Clause 14/16 distinction: Congress knew what it had been given and used exactly those powers. The power to regulate was never in its hands.
Furthermore, the Act was never operative. It imposed duties with no enforcement mechanism. Within a decade it was universally ignored. It was explicitly repealed by the Dick Act of 1903, which replaced the constitutional Militia with a federally controlled National Guard. The Act's universal non-enforcement and eventual repeal confirm the 234-year default — Congress attempted its Clause 16 duties and failed even at those. The People's reserved regulatory power remained untouched throughout.
The Arming Duty: Congress's Constitutional Obligation — And Its Betrayal.
Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 grants Congress power to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the Militia. Johnson's Dictionary defines the operative words with precision. "Provide" means to procure beforehand; to get ready; to supply; to furnish. "Arm" means to furnish with weapons of offence. Read in plain English: Congress was given the duty to supply the Militia with weapons. Not to mandate that citizens supply themselves. Not to impose a burden on the People and call it congressional provision. To procure. To get ready. To furnish.
The Militia Act of 1792 did the opposite. It required every free male citizen aged 18 to 45 to personally purchase a musket, bayonet, cartridge box, and equipment — at his own expense, from his own resources, with no supply, no reimbursement, and no support from the government that had just claimed to have "provided for arming" him. Congress performed none of the duties the word "provide" imposes. It issued a mandate. It imposed a cost. It transferred its own constitutional obligation onto the backs of the People it was supposed to serve, dressed the transfer in legislative language, and called it compliance.
This is not constitutional governance. This is the conscription of private wealth. "Provide for arming" means Congress arms the Militia. The 1792 Act means the Militia arms itself while Congress takes credit. These are not different means to the same end. They are categorically different acts. One fulfills the duty. The other inverts it — transferring downward a constitutional burden that belongs to Congress, onto ordinary citizens who had just finished fighting a war and were being told to spend their own money maintaining the armed force the republic required.
The Militia Act of 1792 was therefore not merely insufficient — it was repugnant to the Constitution. Article VI, Clause 2 declares that only laws "made in Pursuance" of the Constitution are supreme. A law that commands citizens to bear a burden the Constitution explicitly assigns to Congress is not made in Pursuance of anything. It contradicts the constitutional command it purports to fulfill. It is void ab initio. The People's universal non-compliance was not civic failure. It was the constitutionally correct response to a statute that had no binding force from its inception, because a law that inverts a constitutional duty rather than discharging it has no claim to obedience under Article VI.
Congress had demanded what it had no constitutional authority to demand. A demand issued in contradiction of an explicit constitutional assignment does not become law by being written in statutory form. The Act bound no one from the moment it was signed, because it was not made in Pursuance of the Constitution — it was made in opposition to the Constitution's plain command that Congress provide, not conscript.
This analysis does not create a new dependency. The People's obligation to comprise the Militia does not wait on Congress having first fulfilled its arming duty. These are parallel constitutional obligations running in opposite directions: Congress must supply; the People must constitute. Congress's breach of its supply duty does not extinguish the People's natural right — secured by the Second Amendment itself — to arm and organize themselves. The Act's failure on the arming duty is one dimension of the 234-year default. It proves that Congress was in breach of its own Clause 16 obligations from the beginning, and that its breach was not merely a failure of will but an affirmative constitutional violation, compounding the default the People's reserved regulatory power is now called to remedy.
These Regulations do not replace what Congress must provide. They establish the framework within which Congress's organizing, arming, and disciplining must operate. The 1792 Act represents the discipline these Regulations require a Constitution-compliant Congress to produce — once such a Congress exists to produce it. Until then, these Regulations stand as the People's fulfillment of what the Constitution has always required: a well regulated Militia, necessary to the security of a free State.
1.5 Unified and Inclusive Framework
The militia operates as one entity under the People’s regulations, exclusively enforcing Union laws, per the Second Amendment. All units follow this framework for Union laws. All State actions regarding the militia—including officer appointments and training—shall faithfully execute the unified regulations established by the People. No state may create local regulations or rules that modify, contradict, or fragment the national framework whom all militia fall under. Membership is open to all lawful U.S. citizens who are physically and mentally capable of performing militia duties, ensuring broad inclusion consistent with the Bill of Rights, without restrictions based on age, race, gender, or other characteristics unless they impair serviceability, serviceability is always first priority.
1.6 Organization and Oversight
Congress governs such Part of the Militia as may be employed in the Service of the United States, exercising command authority during federal service under Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 (governing such Part as may be employed) when called forth under Clause 15 (executing Laws, suppressing Insurrections, repelling Invasions). This governance includes tactical deployment, mission assignments, rules of engagement during federal operations, coordination with the Executive branch as Commander-in-Chief, and discipline for federal service violations. Congress also provides for organizing, arming, and disciplining the Militia (separate Clause 16 authority), supplying resources but not regulating the Militia's internal structure, which remains under the People's authority per the Second Amendment and Tenth Amendment. Congressional governance is temporally limited: it applies only during actual federal service and terminates upon completion of Clause 15 duties. Any exercise of governance authority beyond these temporal and substantive limits exceeds Congress's delegated powers, constitutes an infringement upon the free state, and shall be nullified by the Militia.


This governance authority is strictly temporal and mission-specific. It does not diminish the People's perpetual regulatory authority over the Militia's existence, membership, and constitutional purpose, which is reserved under the Second and Tenth Amendments and exercised through these Regulations.


States appoint officers and oversee training, as authorized by Clause 16, in accordance with and subordinate to the People's regulatory framework for free state security. The People regulate and oversee the militia, ensuring its exclusive enforcement authority remains accountable. to constitutional principles, maintaining its identity as a force "of the People, by the People, and for the People.". 


Collaboration with State Authorities:
The Free State Militia, regulated by the People as the whole body beyond State oversight, coordinates with State authorities to fulfill its constitutional mandate under the Second Amendment and Article I, Section 8. This includes:
         * Partnering with states for training and command, as appointed by state authorities per Article I, Section 8, Clause 16, during Federal or State emergencies, or when called forth by States to execute State laws consistent with the Constitution and the reserved powers of the Tenth Amendment.
         *  Aligning Militia efforts with State initiatives that uphold the security of a free state, including support for State-led resistance to unconstitutional Federal actions.
         * Engaging State legislatures to defend the Constitutional order and the powers reserved to the States and the People under the Ninth and Tenth Amendments.

(c) Coordination Mandate: All Militia operations involving private conduct shall:

         3. Establish joint command when both federal and State interests are implicated
(d) The Channel of Reserved Authority: 


The People's reserved regulatory power flows into and animates the constitutional structure through the following channels:
         1.  Through the Body of the Militia: The Regulations are ratified and upheld by the armed People themselves, the very body whose existence is declared necessary.
         2.  Through State Apparatus: State-appointed officers (§1.3.2) and state-conducted training become the implementers of the People's unified regulations, harmonizing reserved and delegated authority.
         3. Through Congressional Provision: Congress's delegated power to 'provide for' organizing and arming (§1.4) is directed to fulfill the requirements set by the People's regulations.Thus, the exercise of the reserved power does not ignore the Constitution's structure but completes it, providing the essential 'regulation' that the text requires but leaves to the People to establish.

No state coordination activity in the Phase 3 category shall be represented to any state official as currently authorized or currently operative. Phase 2 advocacy is not Phase 3 operation. The distinction must be maintained in all Militia communications with state officials.
1.6A Relationship with the President and Executive Authority
1.6A.1 Constitutional Basis for Presidential Command
Article II, Section 2, Clause 1 of the Constitution provides: "The President shall be Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States, and of the Militia of the several States, when called into the actual Service of the United States."
This clause establishes that upon a lawful call by Congress under Article I, Section 8, Clause 15, the federalized portion of the Militia passes under the command authority of the President of the United States for the duration of such service.
1.6A.2 Integration, Not Competition
The Free State Militia affirms that its relationship with the President is one of integrated constitutional function, not competition or parallel authority. The constitutional design operates as a unified system:
         * Congress provides for calling forth the Militia (Art. I, §8, Cl. 15)
         * The President commands the Militia when called forth (Art. II, §2, Cl. 1)
         * The Militia executes the Laws of the Union under that command
         * The People retain perpetual regulatory authority over the Militia's character and standards (Second & Tenth Amendments)
No provision in these Regulations diminishes, conflicts with, or supersedes the President's constitutional authority to command the federalized Militia.
1.6A.3 Duty of the President
The President's duty under Article II, Section 3 to "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed" is properly discharged through the constitutionally-designated instrument—the Militia called forth by Congress. Faithful execution requires using the means the Constitution provides, not creating alternative instruments (such as federal law enforcement agencies) not delegated by the Constitution. A President who calls upon the Militia to execute the Laws of the Union, rather than unconstitutional agencies, fulfills both the letter and spirit of the Article VI oath.
1.6A.4 Duty of the Militia
When the Militia is called into federal service by a constitutionally-compliant Congress, it shall obey the lawful commands of the President as Commander in Chief. The Militia shall not resist, obstruct, or delay lawful orders issued within the President's constitutional authority for the purposes enumerated in Article I, Section 8, Clause 15: executing the Laws of the Union, suppressing insurrections, and repelling invasions.
1.6A.5 Distinction Between Office and Occupant
Nothing in this section shall be construed to require obedience to a President who, having received actual notice of these Regulations and the constitutional violations identified herein, knowingly and willfully continues to:
(a) Enforce or perpetuate fiat currency in violation of Article I, Section 10;
(b) Command or direct non-Militia federal enforcement agencies operating without Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 authority;
(c) Issue orders that would require the Militia to violate the Bill of Rights or other explicit constitutional commands.
In such circumstances, the President acts as an oath-breaker (as defined in Section 13.2.1) and forfeits the authority to command. The Militia's duty is to the Constitution and the office, not to any occupant who has abandoned both. This paragraph implements the principle that no official, including the President, is above the Constitution.
1.6A.6 Restoration, Not Usurpation
The Free State Militia seeks not to assume executive power but to restore the conditions under which a constitutionally-compliant President can faithfully execute the laws through the instrument the Constitution provides. When constitutional governance is restored, the Militia stands ready to serve under presidential command as the nation's first line of defense and the primary executor of the Laws of the Union, exactly as the Framers intended.
1.6B War Powers and the Constitutional Division of Authority
1.6B.1 Constitutional Framework
The Constitution establishes a deliberate division of war powers:
(a) Congress possesses the exclusive power "To declare War" (Article I, Section 8, Clause 11). This power is legislative, collective, and representative—requiring the consent of both Houses. No other entity may initiate offensive war.
(b) The President, as Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy and of the Militia when called into federal service (Article II, Section 2, Clause 1), directs military operations once war is authorized. This power is executive, unitary, and operational.
(c) The Militia is the entity designated to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions (Article I, Section 8, Clause 15). When called forth for war under a proper congressional declaration, the Militia may be federalized and organized as land forces (Section 4.9).
1.6B.2 Distinctions Among Uses of Force
Four distinct constitutional situations must be distinguished:
