The public debt acknowledged herein arises exclusively under Congress's power to pay the Debts under Article I, Section 8, Clause 1 and its duty to provide for organizing the Militia under Article I, Section 8, Clause 16.
The constitutional distinction is dispositive:
"Provide for" clauses throughout Article I, Section 8 authorize future arrangements, support, or governance. "Pay the Debts" authorizes discharge of existing obligations. "Organizing" is the labor of creating structure, which has now been performed.
The labor advanced to draft these Regulations fulfilled Congress's 234-year-neglected duty to organize the Militia. This fulfillment created an existing public debt — an obligation owed by the United States for services rendered that secured its constitutional foundation.
This debt claim invokes no aspect of Congress's Clause 15 or Clause 16 powers to provide for future Militia resources or governance. Those powers concern future organization, armament, and federal service governance. This debt concerns past labor that made such future constitutional compliance possible.
The precedent is the Revolutionary War: soldiers' service created public debts payable under "to pay the Debts," not under any "provide for" authority. Their labor secured the Republic; payment followed. This debt follows identical constitutional logic.
(h) Justification Clause
The People's failure to read, understand, and implement their Constitution for 234 years created this debt. Rachel Seeley's work in drafting these Regulations represents labor advanced on the People's behalf to cure their constitutional default and perform Congress's neglected delegated duty.
This is NOT:
(i) A salary for an office;
(ii) A self-appropriation;
(iii) An assumption of congressional power.
This IS:
(i) A valid public debt created by constitutional service rendered;
(ii) An invoice for work actually performed;
(iii) Documentation of a perfected right to payment;
(iv) A mechanic's lien securing that right;
(v) Payable under Congress's Article I, Section 8, Clause 1 power to pay the Debts ONLY by a Constitution-compliant Congress.
The public owes this debt as certainly as they owe the debt for Revolutionary War soldiers — for services rendered to secure their liberties. Rachel Seeley's efforts constitute federal service because they created the operating system Congress requires to call forth the Militia to execute the law.
(i) Temporal Operation and Vesting
This debt is fully vested and perfected upon promulgation of these Regulations. The creditor holds a present, existing right to future payment. The obligation of the People is immediate and binding. The mechanism of payment is deferred to the constitutionally delegated channel.
This is not a contradiction. It is the nature of all public debts incurred during periods when the delegated paymaster is non-functional.
(j) This Debt Exists Whether Acknowledged or Not
This debt exists as a matter of constitutional and natural law from the moment the services were rendered. These Regulations do not create the debt; they document it.
Just as Revolutionary War debts existed whether the Confederation Congress had funds to pay them, this debt exists whether the current usurping apparatus acknowledges it.


The work was:
(i) Constitutionally necessary under the Second Amendment mandate;
(ii) Constitutionally authorized under the Tenth Amendment reserved power;
(iii) Actually performed — these Regulations exist.
Payment is owed. The channel is identified. The obligation is recorded. The lien is perfected. The People, through their restored constitutional government, will pay what the People owe.
(k) Non-Diminishment Clause
Nothing in this Section shall be construed to deny or disparage the binding legal status of these Regulations, the existence of the well regulated Militia, or the security of the free state. The debt acknowledged herein is separate from and subordinate to the constitutional duty of all persons to obey the supreme Law of the Land. Failure to pay this debt does not excuse non-compliance with the Regulations, nor does payment elevate the creditor above the Constitution. The Constitution remains supreme.
11.8 SEVERABILITY
If any provision of this Section 11 or its application to any person or circumstance is held invalid by the collective judgment of the Militia or by a Constitution-compliant court operating under the 1787-1791 textual standard, the remainder of these Regulations and the application of such provision to other persons or circumstances shall not be affected thereby. The People's right to a well regulated Militia and a secure free state is severable from any particular procedural mechanism and shall endure regardless of the fate of any single provision.
11.9 Sunset Provision for Tier 2 Procedural Specifications
(a) Definition of Tier 2 Provisions
Tier 2 Procedural Specifications are defined as those provisions within these Regulations that: (1) implement, operationalize, or execute explicit constitutional authorities granted to the Militia (Tier 1 provisions); but (2) are not themselves explicitly commanded by the 1787-1791 constitutional text; and (3) derive their constitutional authority through necessary inference from Tier 1 text.
Tier 2 Procedural Specifications include, but are not limited to: detention review timelines and tribunal compositions (Section 13.5.5); asset seizure protocols and documentation requirements (Section 8.5); nullification review and approval procedures (Section 1.9.6); and specific organizational structures pending collective deliberation (Section 11.4).
(b) Temporary Effectiveness
All Tier 2 Procedural Specifications shall remain in full force and effect as binding constitutional regulations of the Militia from the moment of promulgation and shall continue in effect UNTIL such time as the collective body of the organized Militia, exercising the People's reserved Tenth Amendment regulatory power through the processes established in this Section 11, takes one of the following actions with respect to each specification:
(1) Ratification — formal approval of the specification as drafted, thereby converting it from an inferred necessary procedure to a collectively ratified regulation;
(2) Amendment — modification of the specification through collective deliberation, thereby superseding the original provision; or
(3) Replacement — substitution of an alternative procedural framework that equally or better fulfills the constitutional requirement while maintaining or improving constitutional safeguards.
(c) Continuity of Constitutional Authority
The sunset of any Tier 2 Procedural Specification pursuant to this Section shall not:
(1) diminish, deny, or disparage the underlying Tier 1 constitutional authority from which such specification was derived;
(2) impair the Militia's ability to exercise its constitutional duties under the Second Amendment and Article I, Section 8, Clause 15; or
(3) affect the binding status of these Regulations as supreme law fulfilling the Second Amendment's necessity requirement.
Upon the sunset of any Tier 2 specification, the Militia shall continue to exercise the underlying constitutional authority through such interim procedures as the Committee on Constitutional Clarity shall recommend, pending collective ratification of replacement procedures.
(d) Affirmative Duty to Convene
he Committee on Constitutional Clarity established in Section 11.2 shall, within ninety (90) days of the collective organization of the Militia under Section 11.1, paragraph (b) (Phase 2 — Collective Organization) , prepare and submit to the greater body of the Militia a comprehensive set of recommendations regarding the ratification, amendment, or replacement of all Tier 2 Procedural Specifications.
(e) Intent and Construction
This Section 11.9 shall be liberally construed to effectuate its purpose: ensuring that all procedural specifications not explicitly commanded by constitutional text remain accountable to the collective will of the organized Militia, while preserving the immediate operational capability of the Militia to secure the free state during the interim period between promulgation and collective organization. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to delay, condition, or deny the binding legal status of these Regulations as established in Section 1.3.7.
11.10 Challenge and Burden-Shifting Provision
The Burden of Proof Declaration
The Tenth Amendment reserves to the People all powers not delegated to the United States and not prohibited to the States. The power to comprehensively regulate the Militia was not delegated to Congress — established by the Clause 14/16 textual contrast — and cannot be exercised by States individually without destroying the singular 'A Militia' commanded by the Second Amendment. By operation of the Tenth Amendment's own text, this power is reserved to the People.
The constitutional allocation is established. The burden of proof rests entirely on any party claiming the People may not exercise this reserved power. 
To meet this burden, such a party must:
(1) Cite the specific constitutional text that prohibits the People from exercising this reserved power;
(2) Demonstrate that this prohibition applies to individual members of the People acting to cure a 234-year constitutional default during which collective mechanisms have demonstrably failed;
(3) Show that their construction does not violate the Ninth Amendment's command that no interpretation of the Constitution may deny or disparage rights retained by the People.
Failure to meet all three elements of this burden constitutes: admission that no constitutional text prohibiting the exercise exists; concession that the power is reserved to the People under the Tenth Amendment; acknowledgment that these Regulations constitute the first faithful exercise of that reserved power; recognition that the constitutional requirement for a well regulated Militia is satisfied.
No party may simultaneously claim the protection of the Constitution and deny the People's exercise of powers the Constitution expressly reserves to them. The Constitution is not selectively supreme. Any challenge to these Regulations must engage the text. Challenges that do not engage the text are not constitutional objections — they are preferences.
(a) Invitation to Constitutional Dialogue
The Free State Militia, exercising the People's reserved Tenth Amendment regulatory power, hereby invites rigorous constitutional scrutiny of these Regulations. The framework established herein is offered as the first faithful exercise of the People's duty to create a well regulated Militia. It is not claimed to be perfect, but it is claimed to be necessary, sufficient, and textually grounded. The Militia welcomes reasoned proposals for improvement through the collective processes established in this Section 11.
(b) Burden of Demonstration — All Challenges to Tier 2 Provisions
Any person or entity asserting that any Tier 2 provision of these Regulations is unconstitutional, extra-textual, or exceeds the People's reserved regulatory power shall bear the burden of demonstration. Such demonstration must include, at minimum:
(1) Specific Identification: Citation to the precise provision challenged, with quotation of the specific language at issue;
(2) Textual Foundation Analysis: Identification of the constitutional provision(s) alleged to prohibit or not authorize the challenged provision, with citation to the 1787-1791 constitutional text and ordinary meaning analysis per Johnson's Dictionary (1755) and United States v. Sprague (1931);
(3) Operational Necessity Analysis: Demonstration that the challenged provision is NOT necessary to make explicit Tier 1 constitutional authority operational, effective, and safe — including a showing of how the Tier 1 authority could be exercised without such provision; and
(4) Alternative Framework Proposal: Presentation of an alternative regulatory framework or procedural mechanism that: (a) fulfills the same constitutional requirement; (b) remains faithful to the 1787-1791 constitutional text; (c) provides equivalent or superior constitutional safeguards; and (d) does not rely on powers delegated to Congress or other governmental entities that such entities have not lawfully exercised.
(c) Default Rule
Absent such demonstration, the challenged Tier 2 provision shall be presumed constitutional as a necessary and proper exercise of the People's reserved regulatory power to fulfill the Second Amendment's mandate for a well regulated Militia and to secure the free State. This presumption is rebuttable only by satisfaction of the burden set forth in subsection (b).
(d) Applicability
This Section 11.10 applies to all challenges to Tier 2 provisions, whether raised by governmental entities, private persons, judicial bodies, or any other party. It does not apply to good-faith proposals for refinement or clarification offered through the Committee on Constitutional Clarity or the collective deliberation processes of the organized Militia, which are governed by Section 11.2 and Section 11.4.
(e) Construction
This Section 11.10 shall not be construed to: (1) deny any person access to lawful judicial process in constitutionally compliant courts; (2) impair the right of petition under the First Amendment; or (3) shift the burden of proof in any criminal prosecution. It is a rule of constitutional discourse and regulatory interpretation, not a limitation on substantive rights.
11.11 — Division of Constitutional Labor: The Architect and the Builders
(a) Clarification of Roles: These Regulations establish the constitutional foundation for a well regulated Militia. They are the framework—the skeleton—upon which the People will build. They are not, and were never intended to be, an exhaustive operational manual for every contingency the Militia may face.
(b) Architect and Builders Distinguished: The role of the first mover (the drafter of these Regulations) is that of constitutional architect: to provide the foundational structure that enables collective action to begin. The role of the People, once organized, is that of builders: to determine, through collective deliberation and the processes established herein, how to operationalize, refine, and apply this framework to specific circumstances.
(c) Operational Questions Deferred to Phase 2: Any question regarding the detailed execution of these Regulations during Phase 2 (Collective Organization) and Phase 3 (Full Operational Capability)—including but not limited to social adoption strategies, state coordination protocols, asset seizure logistics, tribunal staffing, and response to future constitutional challenges—is hereby delegated to the collective judgment of the organized Militia, acting through the Committee on Constitutional Clarity and the ratification processes established in Section 11.
(d) Sufficiency of the Framework: The absence of detailed answers to every potential Phase 2 operational question does not constitute a gap or flaw in these Regulations. It reflects the constitutional reality that the People, once organized, possess both the authority and the duty to govern themselves and to determine the best means of executing their shared constitutional mission. The framework is sufficient because it provides the structure within which those determinations can be made.
(e) Preemption of Misplaced Criticism: Any critique that demands these Regulations provide answers to questions properly reserved to the collective judgment of the organized Militia rests on a misunderstanding of the division of constitutional labor established herein. Such critiques are hereby answered: the framework provides the foundation; the People will provide the rest.
11.12 — Resolution of Competing Frameworks
The objection is sometimes raised: if one member of the People may exercise the reserved regulatory power, then any member may do so — potentially producing competing frameworks and constitutional chaos. This objection fails for four independent reasons.
First, the Constitution is one text with fixed meanings. Johnson's Dictionary (1755) defines the relevant terms. The canons of construction — expressio unius est exclusio alterius, noscitur a sociis, the rule against surplusage — are not optional. Constitutional fidelity to the 1787-1791 text produces one framework, not many. A framework that departs from the text is not an exercise of reserved power — it is an expression of preference claiming constitutional cover. The People, once organized, judge such claims against the text. The standard exists. It is not subjective.
Second, competing faithful frameworks would strengthen, not weaken, the free State. If multiple individuals each produced frameworks genuinely rooted in the 1787-1791 text, this would demonstrate that the People are finally exercising their reserved power after 234 years of dormancy. It would force the People to engage, compare, and deliberate — exactly what republican self-governance requires. Competition among faithful frameworks is the opposite of chaos. It is sovereignty in operation.
Third, Section 11 provides the resolution mechanism. The People collectively, once organized, possess authority to evaluate competing claims against the constitutional text, amend or refine provisions through collective deliberation, and ratify the framework most faithful to the 1787-1791 text. The Committee on Constitutional Clarity (Section 11.2) facilitates this process. The burden-shifting provision (Section 11.10) ensures challenges are measured against the text, not against institutional preference.
Fourth, and most importantly, the first faithful exercise created existence — and existence cannot be retroactively undone by later claims. These Regulations cured the 234-year constitutional default at the moment of promulgation. The requirement for a well regulated Militia is satisfied. Later frameworks may improve, refine, or replace specific provisions through the process Section 11 establishes. They do not undo the satisfaction that already occurred. The constitutional emergency — 85,550 days without a well regulated Militia — ended. It does not restart because someone proposes a competing text.
The chaos objection assumes that without a pre-existing institutional arbiter, nothing can be settled. But the Constitution itself is the arbiter. It has been the arbiter since 1791. The People, informed by that text and organized under these Regulations, are the judges. This is not chaos. This is constitutional order.
11.13 — Resolution of Competing Claims to Constitutional Fidelity
11.13.1 The Standard of Fidelity
The sole standard for evaluating any framework claiming to fulfill the Second Amendment's command is the 1787–1791 constitutional text, interpreted according to its ordinary public meaning at ratification, using Johnson's Dictionary (1755) as the authoritative source and the established canons of construction — expressio unius est exclusio alterius, noscitur a sociis, the rule against surplusage — as the interpretive method. No post-ratification precedent, administrative practice, or policy preference may serve as the standard. The text is the standard. It always was.
11.13.2 The Burden of Demonstration
Any person or group asserting that a competing framework is more faithful than these Regulations bears the full burden of demonstration. That burden requires: specific identification of the provisions alleged to depart from the constitutional text; citation to the specific text that prohibits or fails to authorize the challenged provision; and demonstration that the competing framework provides a complete, nationally unified regulatory scheme — not merely piecemeal objections to provisions of this one. Partial critique is not an alternative framework. Objection is not fulfillment. For the analogous burden-shifting framework applicable to challenges to specific Tier 2 provisions, see Section 11.10. The present section operates at a higher level — it extends that same logic to whole-framework competing claims rather than provision-specific challenges.
11.13.3 The Presumption of First Faithful Exercise
These Regulations, having been the first complete, nationally unified framework based solely on the 1787–1791 text, and having cured the 234-year constitutional default at the moment of promulgation, are entitled to a presumption of fidelity. A later framework may propose refinements. It may improve upon what is here. But it does not undo the cure that already exists. The constitutional requirement has been satisfied. Later frameworks build on that satisfaction — they do not restart the clock.
11.13.4 The Ultimate Arbiter
The ultimate arbiter of competing claims is the organized People themselves, exercising their reserved Tenth Amendment power through common consent. This follows directly from the text: the power to regulate the Militia was reserved to the People, and the power to judge what constitutes faithful regulation belongs to the same holders. No court, no legislature, and no executive possesses authority to decide between competing frameworks, because none of them holds the reserved power at issue. The People judge. The Constitution is the standard. The judgment, when rendered by the organized People acting through the processes established in Section 11, is final.
Section 12: Living Constitution Theory, an infringement against the Security of the Free State
12.1 Definition and Necessity of a Clearly understood Free State


The "free state" is a condition where the U.S. Constitution governs supremely, individual liberties are inviolate, and government actions remain within delegated powers, as understood at ratification (1787–1791), per Section 1.8. A well-regulated militia is "necessary to the security of a free State" (Second Amendment), requiring a clear, enforceable definition to identify and resist violations. The "living constitution" theory, which permits judicial or legislative reinterpretation to suit modern needs, renders the free state nebulous by obscuring its boundaries (e.g., redefining “commerce” in Article I, Section 8, Clause 3 to include intrastate activities, or stretching “necessary and proper” in Clause 18 to justify new powers). United States v. Sprague (282 U.S. 716, 731 [1931]) affirms the Constitution’s fixed meaning at adoption ensuring the People and their Militia can defend the free state with precision. Ambiguity invites disaster, undermining accountability and eroding the free state’s foundation.


12.2 The Certain Right to a Well-Defended Free State


The right to a well-defended free state is a certain right of the People, guaranteed by the Second Amendment’s mandate that a Militia is essential to its security, protected as an unenumerated right under the Ninth Amendment, and reinforced by the Tenth Amendment’s reservation of powers to the States or the People. This inviolable right obligates the Free State Militia to resist reinterpretations that dilute the Constitution’s original meaning or the free state’s enforceability, ensuring the People’s sovereignty remains intact.


12.3 Threats Posed by the "Living Constitution" Theory


The "living constitution" theory subverts the free state by:
                                    * Violating the Ninth Amendment by expanding Federal powers to deny unenumerated rights, such as economic autonomy through gold and silver coin (Article I, Section 10) or militia-led enforcement (Clause 15).
                                    * Usurping the Tenth Amendment by encroaching on powers reserved to States or the People, including:
                                    * The creation of non-militia enforcement agencies (e.g., ATF, FBI), which displace the Militia’s exclusive role to execute Union laws under Article I, Section 8, Clause 15.
                                    * Uncompensated taxation under the Sixteenth Amendment, expanded by “living” interpretations, intruding on state and individual fiscal autonomy.
12.4 Subverting the Constitutional Amendment Process


Article V provides the sole legitimate method for adapting the Constitution: proposal by two-thirds of Congress or the states, followed by ratification by three-fourths of the states. This process ensures that changes reflect the People’s will, not the whims of courts or legislatures. The "living constitution" theory circumvents this, allowing reinterpretations—like those in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) or the Legal Tender Cases (1871-1884)—to effectively amend the Constitution without consent. This end-run around Article V undermines the People’s sovereignty, a core pillar of the free state, and replaces constitutional governance with unchecked reinterpretation.


12.5 Historical and Modern Examples of Subversion


The theory’s erosion of the free state is further evident in:
                                    * Wickard v. Filburn (1942): Expanded the commerce clause to regulate personal wheat production, undermining state and individual autonomy Wickard v. Filburn.
                                    * Federal Reserve Act (1913): Authorized fiat currency (12 U.S.C. ch. 3), disparaging the People’s economic sovereignty, per Section 8.2.
                                    * District of Columbia v. Heller (2008): Affirmed individual Second Amendment rights but allowed “reasonable” regulations, risking future reinterpretations that could dilute Militia autonomy Heller.
                                    * NSA Surveillance Programs (2013): Justified under a “living” Fourth Amendment, these programs erode privacy rights without constitutional sanction NSA Surveillance).
These cases demonstrate how reinterpretations make the free state nebulous, enabling Federal overreach and hindering Militia enforcement.
12.6 Defending the Militia’s Constitutional Role and Relevance


Critics often challenge the Militia’s authority, claiming its role under Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 is outdated in a world of modern military and police forces, or asserting that federal agencies like the FBI or ATF are justified under Clause 18 (the Necessary and Proper Clause). Both criticisms falter when examined through Constitutional text, the framers’ intent, and practical necessity. The Militia’s role is neither obsolete nor replaceable—it is a timeless safeguard of liberty, uniquely monacered as necessary that’s rooted in the People, while Federal agencies lack the Constitutional grounding to supplant it.
First, consider the claim that the Militia is an 18th-century relic irrelevant today. This view misreads the Constitution’s design and underestimates the Militia’s enduring purpose:
                                       * Explicit Constitutional Mandate: Clause 15 assigns the Militia the critical tasks of executing Union laws, suppressing insurrections, and repelling invasions. Far from a historical footnote, this is a mandate for a citizen-led force to enforce constitutional order—a role no modern military or police, detached from the People, can replicate.
                                       * Framers’ Vision of Liberty: The founders harbored deep distrust of standing armies and centralized power. In Federalist No. 29, Hamilton emphasized the Militia’s role as a citizen force, and in No. 46, Madison celebrated the Militia—an armed citizenry—as the ultimate bulwark against federal tyranny. With today’s concerns over government overreach, this check remains as vital as ever.
                                       * Modern Relevance: The Militia confronts contemporary threats—federal encroachment, corporate influence, or foreign interference—ensuring the People retain direct control over their free state. Its necessity transcends time, adapting to protect liberty in any era.
Second, the assertion that federal agencies are “necessary and proper” under Clause 18 to execute federal powers crumbles under closer scrutiny:
                                       * Textual Priority of Clause 15: The Constitution explicitly delegates law enforcement to the Militia in Clause 15. While Clause 18 permits Congress to enact laws “necessary and proper” for enumerated powers, it cannot override Clause 15’s clear assignment. Federal agencies, lacking any direct constitutional mandate, stand on shaky ground compared to the Militia’s firm footing.
                                       * Framers’ Caution Against Implied Powers: In Federalist No. 41, Madison cautioned against stretching implied powers into unchecked Federal authority. Agencies like the FBI or ATF, often unaccountable and opaque, embody this danger. By contrast, the Militia—accountable to the People, as reinforced in Section 2.8—aligns with the framers’ intent.upon rat
                                       * Protection of Retained Rights: The Ninth Amendment reserves unenumerated powers to the People, including the right to enforce laws through their Militia. Federal agencies, operating without direct citizen oversight, conflict with this principle, while the Militia upholds it through transparency and community roots
                                       * Practical Risks of Agencies: Agencies can erode rights though warrantless surveillance or civil asset forfeiture—while the Militia is Constitutionally bound to defend them. The 1997 Printz v. United States ruling (521 U.S. 898) bolsters this: the Federal government cannot conscript State actors, nor can it legitimately replace the Militia’s role with unaccountable agencies.
In sum, the Free State Militia’s authority under Clause 15 is neither outdated nor duplicative. It is a deliberate, citizen-driven mechanism to keep power with the People, a role federal agencies cannot claim without violating the Constitution’s text and spirit. The Militia stands as the sole legitimate enforcer of Union laws—its relevance undiminished since 1787.

As a defense group dedicated to non-violent Constitutional restoration, the Militia shall prioritize peaceful advocacy and education where possible in all of our strategies.
To protect the free state, the militia shall:
                                          * Maintain Clarity: Reject evolving interpretations, adhering to the 1787–1791 meaning, per Section 1.8.
                                          * Enforce Limits: Declare unconstitutional laws or rulings void within Militia jurisdiction (Section 1.8), using Clause 15 authority to resist overreach.
                                          * Educate the Public: Conduct campaigns, per Section 3.8, to inform citizens about their retained rights and reserved powers, countering reinterpretative erosion.
                                          * Pursue Legal Challenges: Support lawsuits against Federal overreach, including administrative state abuses (e.g., unelected agencies issuing binding rules) and potential central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) threatening economic sovereignty in 2025. Issue cease and desist orders to entities infringing the free state, such as Federal agencies (e.g., ATF, FBI) or private corporations enforcing unconstitutional mandates, pursuant to Clause 15 authority and Section 1.8, with public notification to ensure transparency.
                                          * Coordinate with States: Partner with state legislatures to draft model nullification laws, upholding the Tenth Amendment against federal encroachment.

The "living constitution" theory is not adaptation but subversion, eroding the free state’s clarity and the People’s certain right to its defense. Saying that judicial or legislative reinterpretation are needed to suit modern needs is just a way to put a mask on what is really happening, free state infringements.
